Blue-winged teal (Spatula discors) eggs were placed in a laboratory incubator set to a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C] to determine developmental timing under controlled conditions. Hatching occurred after an incubation period of 24.1 days [ab = 24.1 days], a duration consistent with the typical development of small dabbling ducks at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Upon emergence, the wet weight of the newly hatched chicks was recorded with precision, yielding a mean neonatal body mass of 18.3 grams [Wwb = 18.3 grams]. This modest initial mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the embryo at the time of hatching in this species. The chicks, which are precocial, quickly transition to active foraging under the watchful guidance of the female parent. The relatively short incubation period and small hatchling size are adaptations that align with the species' use of ephemeral wetland habitats, where rapid development is advantageous before seasonal water bodies recede.

Field studies and captive observations provide a detailed picture of juvenile development in Spatula discors. After hatching, the downy young experience a phase of rapid somatic growth. A particularly critical developmental milestone is fledging, which occurs at 63 days since birth [tx = 63 days since birth], when the juveniles achieve sustained flight capability. This remarkably early transition to volancy enables the young birds to escape terrestrial predators and follow their mothers to more productive feeding areas. During this period, the growing juveniles consume a diet rich in aquatic invertebrates and seeds, accumulating the protein and energy necessary for feather development. The fledging age is relatively brief for a duck of this size, a life-history trait that likely facilitates the species' ability to produce a single brood within a short breeding season. The coordinated timing of feather growth and muscle maturation underpins this rapid developmental schedule in the Blue-winged teal.

Female Blue-winged teal reach sexual maturation and initiate their first reproductive effort at a specific age. Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal activity and the capacity to breed, is attained at 189 days since birth [tp = 189 days since birth]. However, the actual deployment of this reproductive potential is typically deferred until the following breeding season; the time since birth at first brood is approximately 365 days [tR = approximately 365 days], aligning with an annual breeding cycle. Females typically lay a single clutch consisting of 6 to 15 eggs [N_R_i = single clutch consisting of 6 to 15 eggs], and they only produce one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], a reproductive strategy that prioritizes parental investment in a single brood over multiple nesting attempts. The maximum daily reproduction rate, representing the highest possible output, is 10 eggs per 365 days [Ri = 10 eggs per 365 days], a value that reflects the constraints of single-brood production in this species. This clutch size range is typical for many members of the genus Spatula and reflects the energetic demands of egg production and the prolonged period of brood care that follows hatching.

Adult body mass in Spatula discors exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism, a common pattern among dabbling ducks. The ultimate wet weight for the species ranges from 395 to 478 grams (395-478 grams) [Wwi = 395-478 grams], with females at the lower end and males at the higher end of this range. This size differential is thought to confer advantages in male-male competition for mates, as larger body size can be a decisive factor in agonistic encounters. For their size, Blue-winged teal are relatively light-bodied compared to sympatric diving ducks, an adaptation that facilitates their foraging style of dabbling and tipping-up in shallow waters. The initial wet weight of a newly laid egg is approximately 29 grams [Ww0 = approximately 29 grams], representing a substantial maternal investment. This initial egg mass must supply all the nutrients for the embryo's development through the incubation period, and it sets the stage for the subsequent growth trajectory of the chick.

The maximum lifespan documented for Blue-winged teal under wild conditions reaches approximately 23.2 years [am = approximately 23.2 years], a considerable longevity for a relatively small-bodied waterfowl species. This extended lifespan allows for multiple breeding attempts over an individual's lifetime, buffering against the potential failure of any single reproductive event. Reaching such an age requires the birds to successfully navigate numerous migrations between their breeding grounds in the northern prairies and their wintering areas across the southern United States, Mexico, and Central America. Disease, predation, and hunting pressure represent significant sources of mortality that limit most individuals from achieving this maximum. The combination of a single-egg mass of roughly 29 grams, an 18.3 gram hatchling, and a 395 to 478 gram adult provides a clear picture of the species' growth allometry, while the 24.1 day incubation and 63 day fledging period illustrate the condensed developmental timeline within the annual cycle.
